sweep_summary: Yoruba (in catalog, coded tonal on Crowther 1852 + Hyman 2005/2012, Laniran & Clements 2003). Six title-hits searched. Two read in full from open copies: Nagano-Madsen 1993 (ISCA archive; scanned, scanned) classes Yoruba as a lexical tone language with F0 the correlate and finds only durational (vowel-lengthening) local prominence bound to H/M tones — confirms tonal; Ehineni 2017 (open-access JUL) is OT reduplication templates, three contrastive tones, zero mentions of stress — silent. Hagberg 2006/1993 (read via the archive.org UMI text; SIL PDF and MPG PuRe copy both refused) mentions Yoruba only for its floating-H object clitic and ATR harmony — not about Yoruba stress. Not obtainable: Siertsema 1959 Lingua 'Stress and tone in Yoruba word composition' (Elsevier closed, no OA copy, no abstract; the only item that names stress for Yoruba — HIGH priority to acquire since it could refine the tonal coding); Nagano-Madsen & Bredvad-Jensen 1995 ICPhS (located in the vol. 3 ToC at 3:652 under the corrected title 'Comparing F0 Reset..', but IPA serves no individual 1995 papers; F0-reset intonation study, low priority); Nagano-Madsen 1992 Lund dissertation on mora/duration (no open copy found; low priority). new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Nagano-Madsen 1993 statement (lexical tone carried by F0, no word stress described) and with the catalog's tonal coding of Yoruba (catalog record has an empty rule). Adds an explicit, if brief, statement that stress is not distinctive in Yoruba; does not add placement, weight or secondary-stress detail.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yoruba is a three-tone language (H, M, L on every vowel and syllabic nasal); stress is explicitly stated not to be a distinctive feature of the language, so no word-stress placement rule is given. The statement is a one-line footnote in a coarticulation study, not a phonological analysis of stress.

new_statements.identity_note: Przezdziecki 2005 covers three varieties: Standard Yorùbá (closely related to the Ọ̀yọ́ dialect, spoken in Ìbàdàn and widely as lingua franca), Àkùré Yorùbá (Òndó state) and Mọ̀bà Yorùbá (Ọ̀tùn-Èkìtì, Èkìtì state). The stress footnote (p. 104) refers to Yorùbá in general; the tone description (p. 48) is stated for Standard Yorùbá and extended in general terms to Àkùré and Mọ̀bà.

Yoruba has three contrastive tones-H(igh), M(id), and L(ow), which are generally realized on vowels and sometimes on nasal consonants, i.e. a word may have different lexical meaning depending on whether it is said with a high pitch or a mid pitch or a low pitch. [...] (11) kó (H) (build) / ko (M) (sing) / kò (L) (reject). Therefore tones are like consonants and vowels in Yoruba, since they distinguish the meanings of words like consonants and vowels do. [...] However, there is a restriction on the distribution of the High tone. The High tone occurs in word-initial position only in (marked) consonant-initial words. Except for this minor restriction, tones occur freely in words, without apparent restrictions on word melodies. Two of the three basic tones illustrated above (the High tone and the Low tone) have variants. The High tone (H) is pronounced as a LH (rising tone) contour after a Low tone, and a Low tone is pronounced as a HL (falling tone) contour after a High tone.

sources.quote: p. 30: "where the phonically varying junction takes the form of an 'extra' ó or é with a high tone". p. 37: "First, láàti seems to be bimorphemic in structure because its tonal contour is the type that would normally result when two morphemes lí, with a final high tone, and àti, with an initial low tone, collocate in that order. That is, (49) lí àti → láàti 'in order to' just as (50) lí ɔ̀la → lɔ́ɔ̀la 'in tomorrow', i.e. 'tomorrow' (51) kó ìwé → kóòwé 'gather books' (52) lá àlá → láàlá 'dream a dream', i.e. 'to dream'." p. 35: "In the phonological component, NML will be dropped after any verb immediately following it has been reduplicated. Then the initial consonant of such a reduplicated verb will be deleted either optionally or obligatorily, depending upon the 'high-tone-junction-contracting verb' as well as on the dialect involved." p. 33 (quoting Ida Ward, An Introduction to the Yoruba Language, p. 116): "In every case the lengthening is on a high tone, and would therefore correspond to the reduplicated form which is the verbal noun."

sources.note: Syntactic paper, not a description of the tone system. It argues that the 'high-tone junction' (an extra high-toned vowel between verbs like mɔ̀ 'know', kɔ́ 'learn', fẹ́ 'want' and a following verb-like element) is the remnant of a reduplicated verbal-noun nominalization (Ward's 'lengthening on a high tone'), not a junction between two verbs, so Bamgbose's strong/weak verb classes should be dropped. Tone appears throughout as a property of morphemes: every cited form is tone-marked (high/mid/low), the junction vowel is 'with a high tone', and láàti's contour is derived from lí (final high) + à

tone.quote: In 1911 I recorded with the help of Father Strub, of the Roman Catholic Mission, Agenebode, Southern Nigeria, six Yoruba and three Kukuruku songs, as nearly as they can be represented by our notation, and also the normal rise and fall of the tones in the spoken words. … In the eighth song I am uncertain whether the low tone on me is the singer's normal low tone or a specially deep one, as I had not at the time realised that the intermediate tones between high and low were so numerous. … The small numbers above the vowels show the tones — 1 is high, 4 low.
